title: Finding My Voice: One Woman's Path to Healing from Sexual Abuse
gist: Writer Tonya Nickol recounts surviving childhood sexual abuse by two separate adults, describing how shame, self-harm, and trust issues followed her into adulthood, and reframes her identity from 'victim' to 'survivor' while noting trauma's lasting neurological effects.

insights.claim: Tonya Nickol writes that starting around age four, her mother's boyfriend began sexually abusing her, and later her babysitter's husband also sexually assaulted her, with the abuse continuing until she was 13.
insights.speaker: Tonya Nickol
insights.so_what: Documents a case of repeated abuse by multiple caregiving-adjacent adults over nearly a decade, illustrating how trusted household and childcare relationships can become vectors for prolonged abuse.
insights.quote: When I was around four years old, my mother's boyfriend began sexually abusing me.

insights.claim: Nickol says the abuse finally ended when she was 13 because her sister found the courage to disclose what had been happening to her.
insights.speaker: Tonya Nickol
insights.so_what: Highlights the pivotal role of a third-party disclosure — not adult intervention or the victim's own voice — in ending years of ongoing abuse.
insights.quote: What finally brought it to an end was my sister's courage. She told what had been happening to me.

insights.claim: Nickol also describes childhood emotional and physical abuse from her mother and grandmother, whose unpredictable moods made her feel she had to stay quiet and make herself small to avoid upsetting them.
insights.speaker: Tonya Nickol
insights.so_what: Shows the sexual abuse occurred within a broader household environment of emotional and physical mistreatment, compounding the harm rather than being an isolated incident.
insights.quote: Sometimes, the abuse was emotional; other times, it was physical. I learned to stay quiet, make myself small, and try desperately not to upset anyone.

insights.claim: Nickol writes she was told, directly and indirectly, that she was abused because of how she dressed (in ordinary sundresses), and that she internalized this as shame and began hiding her body under oversized boys' clothing as she got older.
insights.speaker: Tonya Nickol
insights.so_what: Illustrates how victim-blaming messaging from adults directly shapes a child's self-image and coping behavior long after the abuse itself, a pattern relevant to trauma-informed care approaches.
insights.quote: I remember being told, both directly and indirectly, that I was abused because of how I dressed... There was nothing inappropriate about me or my clothing.

insights.claim: Nickol explains that self-harm entered her life as a way to make overwhelming emotional pain tangible and understandable, not as a bid for attention.
insights.speaker: Tonya Nickol
insights.so_what: Offers a first-person corrective to a common misconception about self-harm, useful context for how clinicians, educators, and family members should interpret self-injury in abuse survivors.
insights.quote: Looking back now, I understand that self-harm was never about wanting attention. It was about trying to survive emotions that felt too large to carry alone.

insights.claim: Nickol reports she was raped again as a young adult and kept it secret for years, telling only her husband, because keeping the secret felt easier than sharing it.
insights.speaker: Tonya Nickol
insights.so_what: Shows that childhood abuse patterns of silence and secrecy can persist into adulthood and repeat with subsequent trauma, reinforcing the difficulty of disclosure even for adult survivors.
insights.quote: as a young adult, I was raped. For years, I kept that secret buried deep inside. My husband was one of the only people who knew.

themes.theme: Reframing identity and lasting trauma effects

insights.claim: Nickol describes shifting her self-understanding from seeing herself only as a 'victim' — someone something happened to — to identifying as a 'survivor,' someone who became something through the experience.
insights.speaker: Tonya Nickol
insights.so_what: Articulates a specific cognitive reframe used in trauma recovery, distinguishing passive victimhood from active survivor identity as a turning point in healing.
insights.quote: Being a victim describes what happened to me. Being a survivor describes who I became.

insights.claim: Nickol states that trauma is not a finish line but a lifelong journey, and that the effects of her childhood abuse followed her into adulthood even after the abuse itself ended.
insights.speaker: Tonya Nickol
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the idea that healing has a defined endpoint, relevant to how survivor-support programs and expectations around recovery timelines are designed.
insights.quote: People often imagine healing as a finish line, but it’s really a lifelong journey.

insights.claim: Nickol says trauma physically changes the brain, so specific sounds, smells, or sensations can trigger a return to painful memories years later, and that living with trauma means learning to navigate these triggers rather than expecting them to disappear.
insights.speaker: Tonya Nickol
insights.so_what: Offers a neuroscience-informed explanation for why survivors continue to experience acute trauma responses long after abuse ends, useful for family members and clinicians seeking to understand persistent triggers.
insights.quote: The truth is that trauma changes the brain. Certain sounds, smells, feelings, and experiences become connected to painful memories that can return years down the road.

insights.claim: Nickol says trauma taught her that people are dangerous and vulnerability leads to pain, causing her to build emotional walls that she brought into her marriage, but that she and her husband built trust and safety together over time.
insights.speaker: Tonya Nickol
insights.so_what: Illustrates that trauma-driven relational barriers can be gradually overcome within a committed relationship, offering a hopeful counterpoint to the article's account of lasting harm.
insights.quote: Together, we learned what safety could look like, and we built trust one day at a time.
